name: Dreadlocks

card.summary: A hairstyle of rope-like locked strands that people wear as a long-lasting, low-styling look and cultural statement.
card.note: Heavy or tight locs can contribute to traction hair loss.

quick.overview:
Dreadlocks, or locs, are rope-like strands of hair that form when hair mats and locks together, naturally in very curly hair or through twisting, backcombing or crocheting. People wear them as a distinctive style and as an expression of identity.

The style has a long history in many cultures, from ancient Kerma in Sudan to Rastafari. Dermatology literature discusses it mainly in terms of traction on the scalp.
quick.how: Locs are started by twisting, backcombing or interlocking sections and then maintained with periodic retwisting and washing. They can be grown out over months to years.
quick.risks: A dermatology review links tight hairstyles including locs to traction alopecia, which can become permanent if tension continues. Very heavy locs may cause neck strain.

lead: Dreadlocks, also called locs, are a hairstyle made of rope-like strands of hair. They can form naturally in very curly hair or be created by twisting, backcombing or crocheting.[1]

Wikipedia dates the earliest evidence to the Kerma culture in present-day Sudan, and describes locs in Hindu, Buddhist, Rastafari, Baye Fall and Aladura traditions.[1] They were popularised in the 1960s-70s through Black Power, natural hair movements and reggae.[1]
Dermatology reviews note that dreadlocks are among the tight styles associated with traction alopecia in people who wear them for long periods.[2]

angle.text: Locs give a distinctive look that requires less daily styling once established, and many wearers see them as an expression of heritage or beliefs.

infobox: Rastafari, Baye Fall, Hindu and Buddhist traditions

paras: Very curly hair can knot on its own; other hair types need crochet hooks or backcombing. Wikipedia distinguishes locs from matting caused by neglect.[1]

Locs appear in ancient Egyptian art and later in Ethiopian, Sufi and Yoruba-Christian traditions; Rastafari adopted them in the 1930s.[1] Workplace and school bans led to US CROWN Act laws, starting with California in 2019.[1]

A 2018 review states that traumatic hairstyles including tight braids and dreadlocks raise the risk of traction alopecia, which can progress to scarring alopecia if tension continues.[2] A 2025 review of Black hair care notes that dermatologists lack many hair-care recommendations for styles such as locs.[3] A case report describes a fatal accident in which a man's locs were caught in machinery.[4]
Reviews of traction alopecia list dreadlocks among higher-risk styles.[2] No trial has tested locs as an intervention.

timeline.event: Rastafari movement adopts locs in Jamaica.[1]
